utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Judge Van Den Wyngaert is unfortunately ill and not able to sit today. Judge Thelin and I will continue sitting under the rule. Mr. Moore, you were on you feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. It's a small matter, or two matters, actually. Your Honour may remember that I had broached the topic of the defendants being interviewed in Belgrade at the courts. And they giving accounts to the either investigating judge or to the judge at that time. I was certainly intending to put them in as evidence, not for the truth of their content, quite the reverse, but the fact that they should be admissable and part of the case. Your Honour, I've had an opportunity of looking at the jurisprudence. If one looks at it simply, I was concerned about the doctrine of estoppel. If the defendants give evidence, I would wish to use those documents potentially for cross-examination, and that being the case if the court took a preliminary view that those documents were prima facie admissable, subject to argument, if any of the defendants give -- if any of the defendants give evidence, then I would not seek to produce a motion or present a motion to the Court, but to leave it until such times as it may become necessary. So, in simple terms, I would seek to use the documents for cross-examination if the defendants gave evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do we understand that they have -- copies of them have been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, they've got copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't that the Chamber needs to hear you. The position is one that's fairly clear. The Prosecution is confirming that although it will be closing its case without tendering some statements said to have been made by the accused, that should they give evidence it would or may seek to rely upon those for the purposes of cross-examination. This is essentially one of notice and avoiding any suggestion of surprise in the tendering of the -- or use of the documents during cross-examination. And given that the existence of these has been disclosed to the Defence, that they've been provided copies, and that Mr. Moore has indicated that he has them and his intention, I think, there can be no question but that the Defence is fully on notice of their existence and it may be that they will be used and no possibility of the Prosecution being estopped from their use could properly arise. So, Mr. Moore, it is sufficient, I think, if it was left on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I deal with a second topic; it's simply this: We have the witness P-002, we had served on us, I believe this morning, 10 documents which have been compiled by that witness. Two of them at the moment have been translated, the other eight we have not yet any translations for them. That being the case, I would make application that either we adjourn the case so that we can have some form of translation and the witness have an opportunity at least of seeing them, or secondly, and this is what concerns me, is that the witness himself is in personal difficulty time-wise, and there may be difficulties if the Court were minded to grant an adjournment, it may create difficulties for him. If that were the case, and I will speak to the witness, then I would make application firstly for an adjournment, if the witness is not able to adjourn for that period for him to commence his evidence today and the documents that have not been translated to be removed or excluded by way of cross-examination because they have not conformed in any way whatsoever with the either directive given by the Court or the spirit of the Court in relation to disclosure of documentation. But I need to speak to the witness to see whether he would be able to stay an extra day, if that was necessary. I'm very aware of the Court timetable, I am very aware that I have three experts next week who are on firm timetables. Fortunately we have no other witness, apart from P-002 this week, and if there was a short adjournment then it would mean still that we would be able to stick to the timetable as we had proposed next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it possible, while we hear from counsel on the submission that inquiries could be made now whether the witness is able to stay another day and what the problem is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. He has gone back to his hotel to change, he was here for proofing for a short period this morning. He is not well. He has had a part of his foot amputated, and things are difficult for him health-wise. He will be coming back in, I think, about the next half hour, and I will be able to speak to him then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, yes. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone. I think that what my learned friend has said, first of all, relates to the Defence team, I assume, to Mr. Radic. I am not going to speak about that. I would just like to remind everyone that perhaps this week on Friday, if all of the Defence agree, can start with the evidence of the expert Theunens. I think that we agreed last Friday that, if it suits everyone, Mr. Theunens could begin his testimony on Friday. I would just like to mention one more thing, briefly, now that I do have the floor, and that is a fact concerning the indisputable facts which, as we have heard, have still not reached Their Honours. You will recall that we insisted earlier that those facts that we did reach agreement on with our learned friends on the other side should be submitted to Their Honours possible. And we agreed on those facts and signed them on the 16th of March, 2006. After that on the 27th of April, 2006 we received notice that Their Honours were seeking some clarifications in relation to those facts and on the 10th of May, 2006, we responded positively to five questions from this motion. And we believe that on the 10th of May the final version was agreed and signed by the parties. On behalf of all of the Defence teams I must say that we are all concerned that this has still not reached Their Honours and I think that my learned friends would need to submit that to the Trial Chamber immediately. If there are some additional facts that we can discuss, the Defence is always prepared until the end of the proceedings to discuss them, but I believe that the number of facts that have already been agreed should be submitted as soon as possible to the Trial Chamber. As I have said we have reached agreement on them over a month ago. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. We see that there is a problem now in relation to Witness P-002. The witness testified before, before this Trial Chamber -- actually before this Tribunal as well as before the Belgrade court, and there were never any problems before during the testimony. We know about the health problems of this witness from earlier, but we believe that the request to delay his testimony has nothing to do with that, but it's more related to the problem of some new documents appearing. This is not the first time that the Prosecution is having a problem in relation to documents that witnesses bring documents shortly before they are proofed by the Prosecution. This has obviously happened again in this case, and that can make the cross-examination more difficult in a certain way. I believe, though, that regardless of the fact that my colleague Borivoje Borovic will be questioning the witness, the position of the Radic Defence is that the examination-in-chief of this witness can begin and then we will see whether the documents will be translated in time and then it will also be up to the Trial Chamber to decide whether the documents would be acceptable, if the Prosecution should wish to tender them into evidence. This is all that I have to say so far, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does this concern you, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything that limits the scope of my cross-examination is of concern to me, but I would just like to move into private session, because of the witness, if possible, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The issue is -- arises because of non-compliance with the orders that have been made for the notice of materials to the opposing party. In this case the consequences of that are not such that in the Chamber's view it is necessary to go so far as to exclude the proposed documents from evidence, as Mr. Moore ventured as one solution. So that -- in the Chamber's view that should not be the consequence. However, it is clear that Mr. Moore should have time to secure at least quick, working translations, be able to understand himself the nature of the documents, and that the witness should have an ability to review those articles and in the course of proofing be able to discuss their content with counsel for the Prosecution. In our view, that would require that his evidence start on Wednesday rather than tomorrow. There is one further possibility to allow a little further time, because if we started him on Wednesday we would certainly have to be very controlled in our time if we are to hear the expert witness Theunens on Friday. Now, that is one alternative, and the Chamber would be prepared to make this order on the occasion, in the circumstances, his evidence in chief could start today but there would be leave to the Prosecution to further proof the witness between the end of hearing today and Wednesday in respect of the new documents. Now, that can lead to problems and difficulties in way of procedure and concern that there may have been too much discussion by Prosecution, so we would frankly prefer that the start of the evidence be on Wednesday. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask, please, for it to be Wednesday. I anticipate I will be able to deal with the witness, given a fair wind we are all day on Wednesday and Thursday, I should be finished between two and a half and three hours, so that will be two sessions, which give the Defence twice that amount in cross-examination and still not impact on to Theunens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will hear the earlier witness who is being recalled today. The evidence of the next witness, P-002 will commence Wednesday morning. And we will hear the witness Theunens commencing Friday morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you will allow me, just one more thing. I will try not to take up too much time from the cross-examination of the next witness. My learned friend Mr. Moore said that the 48-hour rule was violated. I am saying that because I would like to establish for the following witnesses that are still to come, and also for witnesses that will appear in the Defence case, exactly what the dead-line is. I recall that shortly before the testimony of witness Trifunovic, Your Honours warned the Defence that because of the importance of military experts the dead-line to establish -- to provide documents would be changed to 48 hours. Up until then the dead-line was 24 hours, but P-002 is not such a witness, and that is why the Radic Defence assumed that the dead-line was 24 hours, in view of a very tight schedule for these days, and in relation to the time we found out when P-002 would begin his testimony, this is what we did. We also knew that today we would only have witness Grujic, and also we expected the examination-in-chief to begin of P-002 with the cross-examination beginning the day after that. So we believe then that we did meet the 24-hour dead-line rule. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are quite correct in your statement, Ms. Tapuskovic, that this not being an expert witness, notice of 24 hours was required. What is particularly wrong and difficult in this case is that there was a document provided or documents provided not translated into the language of the Court, which would mean that it would be of no use to the Chamber and no use to Mr. Moore. And while the minimum requirement is 24 hours, if there is a number of documents so that the volume becomes large, it is obviously unreasonable to expect others to master a large volume of documents in just 24 hours. We keep the time as short as 24 hours so that a document which comes very late to your notice is important can be served with just 24-hours notice. But if you know that you have a large number of documents, you must ensure that they are translated and because of the volume, there is more there than can reasonably be assimilated and dealt with by your opponents in just 24 hours. Very well. Thank you. We will move on. Mr. Moore, before you leave, I think it would be useful if we could mention looking ahead. Time notice would be of value to all counsel, that we anticipate of course that evidence will finish in -- on the Friday after next Friday. It's not known to the Chamber whether there is in contemplation a Rule 98 bis motion. If that is in contemplation, the Chamber would anticipate hearing the oral submissions which are now called for by the rule on the following Wednesday, the 28th of June. And it would anticipate that the Defence should have no more than one and a half sitting sessions on that day for their submissions, and that the Prosecution would have a similar time, so that we would conclude the submissions in the course of that day. We would hear submissions at another time. Just how much time the Defence would anticipate needing in preparation, and this affects probably Mr. Vasic more than anybody else because he's first in line, but we, as we have indicated throughout, have in mind a fairly quick turn-around from Prosecution case to Defence. And we will therefore hear quickly peoples' views at a time when it's convenient about that, and we will plan the timetable from the 28th of June in light of that. But do be on notice of the 28th of June for Rule 98 business, if it's thought that there should be such a motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, and welcome back. Could I -- I think it would be a preferable precaution in view of the time that you have been away if you were to make the affirmation again. If you have the affirmation card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, this witness is simply recalled for the purpose of completing cross-examination. I see no dissent from that. I think it's over to you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, good afternoon. My name is Novak Lukic, I'm one of the Defence counsel of Veselin Sljivancanin, and on behalf of his Defence team I will be putting questions to you. We are the reason, our team is the reason you had to return to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First I want to see whether you have the binder in front of you, the one that we used during your previous testimony, with the index of all documents?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First I will be putting you questions about your biography, and that was covered in examination-in-chief, and also Mr. Vasic touched upon that. The questions will pertain to your work at MUP and also your work within the commission for detainees and missing persons. So we are now referring to the period up to 1991, when you used to work at MUP, and you will agree with me, won't you, that every Ministry of the Interior has normally two sections, one as public law and order and the other one is state security, if we may call it that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the general principle of organisation, there were some services that could not fit that description. Some services fell under both those sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the main activities of the MUP are aimed at these two sectors, public law and order and state security?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in general terms, yes. But there were certain crimes which were directed against the constitutional law and order and could fall both under public law and order and State Security Services.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would we agree that the main task of state security is to preserve the constitutional organisation and order of Croatia, because you worked for the MUP of Croatia, but that also pertained to all other ministries of the interior and other republics; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the main task of the public Security Services is to preserve public law and order. Is that their main task?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the main task, yes. But that task also has elements that could fall under the other sector, that of state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief, and in cross-examination you said that you were specialised for anti-terrorist activities; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think back in 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you served in Osijek and that region, right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I carried out tasks in the territory of the town of Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said to Mr. Vasic that you also participated partially in the voluntary surrender of weapons during that period of time, which was carried out in various villages. You personally, and your department, did you send to your superiors reports about weapons that were distributed along the party lines?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, party lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For example, did you know that at that time the weapons were distributed by the activists of the HDZ to the supporters of that party and other activists?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that all the information we collected at the time relating to any arming of any groups, all such information was sent up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what you said to Mr. Vasic, but my question was, do you remember specifically sending reports to your superiors about the arming of the HDZ supporters in Osijek at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, it's been quite a while, many years have passed, but I'm sure that there must have been at least one report dealing with that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You served in that position in October of 1990, right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Ante Gilje is?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But I know him from the later period of time, or rather I heard of him later. He is a member of the Croatian army who worked for the military police of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what his role was in October of 1990?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly wouldn't know what he did at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Ivan Zovak is?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you've probably heard of Tomislav Mercep?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of him and I also know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was his position in October of 1990 in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer accurately, but I think that he was a national defence secretary or something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Vitezit 60 is?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain it to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a type of explosive. One used for industrial purposes, so it wasn't intended for military purposes but was used for industrial purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, in accordance with the then regulation in force, was there any need for any political party to be in possession of such an explosive and to distribute it to other individuals? Were political parties allowed to be in possession of that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only no political parties were allowed to possess that, but also no physical person without proper permits could be in possession of such explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we now please put on the screen document 3D01-0063. You will now see a document; you may be familiar with it, and maybe not. English translation is 0064, but could we please see the B/C/S version? Thank you. Have you ever seen this document, Mr. Grujic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, take a look at it. Go over it.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no need for that. We have it in our system, you just need to acquaint yourself with the document. Let me tell you what this is about. Receipt, I hereby state that I received from the Osijek HDZ from Branimir Glavas Vitezit 60 explosive for the needs of the HDZ branch offices in our municipalities. One to Ante Gilje from Nustar took over this explosive for the municipality of Vinkovci, 75 kilograms of explosive, and then Ivan Zovak from Zupanja took it for the municipality of Zupanja, 100 kilograms of explosive, and then the third person is Tomislav Mercep from Vukovar, who took it over for the municipality of Vukovar, 100 kilograms of explosives, and all of them signed this document and it's dated 21st of October in Osijek. So you say that you never seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We received it from the OTP. In view of the job that you had at the time, what would be your comment? Don't you think that this illegal to say the least?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to tell you about the job that I performed at the time, and give you my comment in view of the job that I held. Had I known about this document at the time, I would have acted in accordance with the regulations in force at the time, and I would have informed my superiors up the chain of command within my service. Naturally they would have taken action and taken steps to prosecute these people in relation to this explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you say to us that you are not familiar with this document, but you are telling us that you would have initiated action had you known about this. Would you agree with me that at the time this was not only unlawful, but also unconstitutional? If it was your job to carry out anti-terrorist activities, would you agree that this was an omission in your work at the time, the fact that you didn't know about this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it an omission, you do understand that one cannot know everything and when we do have knowledge, then we take proper action. Then at the time, together with the members of the JNA Security Service we conducted an action to seize weapons from, if we're now talking along -- about ethnic affiliation, then we seized weapons from ethnic Croats in all instances where we were aware of the facts. So I'm telling you that I didn't know about this; had I known about this, I would have done something about it. There were people above me, and my job was to collect information and to send it up the chain of command to relevant superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. You told us about your joint action with the JNA aimed at seizing unlawfully-held weapons. Tell me, please, in October of 1990, what position did Glavas hold?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was the TO secretary in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about his party role?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't be able to tell you, I was never a party member myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you were in state security, I thought that you might know this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't look into anybody's party affiliation. It is contrary to democratic principles, it was so back then and nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you have to ask you, if the job of state security, one of the jobs of state security is to combat terrorism, and if in certain political parties there are individuals who engage in unlawful conduct, wouldn't it be true that the job of state security is also to monitor the activities of political parties if there is reason to believe that there are some individuals engaging in unlawful activity there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way, yes. But you know that the state security was organised in a different way, and that internal affairs were within the jurisdiction of another service. And it was the department for internal security that was in charge of these things, and you must know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I won't go further into this, but let me just say that at the time you had a very successful career, your career was on a fast track, you were promoted very quickly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree with that. If you go back and look at my CV and you will see that back in 1972 I was an ordinary policeman, and then I was promoted by one level every four years, and this is how I became an inspector. When I moved from the Ministry of the Interior to the Croatian army, that was not a promotion, I remained at the same level, in accordance with the then regulations. So factually, that meant that my rank was a level below than what I held at the Ministry of the Interior. I don't think that this is a promotion at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was my view analysing your biography. Another question that I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you do, before you leave this issue, there's been a lot of mention of October in connection with the receipt. Is it that the receipt is -- has a date or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, I didn't want to read the entire document because we have it in e-court. The document is dated 21st of October, 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document will become Exhibit 560.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one more question from that period coming as a result of your answer to a question from Mr. Vasic. When we're talking about Labrador affairs and your comment in relation to that, you said you don't know about eavesdropping, but I know they were eavesdropping me. I'm intrigued now, who is it that you think eaves dropped on you, when and why?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I was the subject of eavesdropping.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Followed.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Followed, these two are very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I would like to clarify this for you and also for Their Honours. The word Labrador was mentioned. This was a group of intelligence officers that worked within the existing structure for other structures, if I can comment like that. In response to the question whether I knew about the Labrador group, I said that I did not know about it, I wasn't overseeing it, they were probably overseeing me, because they were within my organisation monitoring what that organisation was doing, but we didn't know about it, this is something that was confirmed later, and then the matters were processed and what happened, happened. So to clarify, the Labrador group is a group that worked within the existing structure for some other structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you just assume that that was what they were doing or you know that for certain?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had to know what we were doing, and I mention that because the chief of that group, Mr. Drazen, was the chief. So he must have known what they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's move to a new topic. I'm going to put several questions to you about your work in the commission for detainees and missing persons. One of the tasks of that commission was to participate in the exchange negotiations in relation to prisoners on the territory of the whole of Yugoslavia; is that correct? I don't believe that Slovenia and Croatia figured much there, but one of the tasks of your commission was to negotiate with the commissions from Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And I also omitted to say with also representatives of temporarily occupied territories, they also had their own commission and their prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about that as well. You actively participated in the work of the commission in 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in May I was appointed the president of the government commission for detainees and missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also negotiated with representatives of the commission for exchanges of Republika Srpska and Herceg Bosna, the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also negotiated with Amir Masovic, probably also with General Radinovic, am I right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with General Radinovic, but with Amir Masovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just like to add my question on page 20 -- actually, page 21, line 1, I said the HVO, and what I said before that was Herceg Bosna, and this is not recorded in the transcript. Who did you negotiate in that period of 1993, 1994, that was from the Yugoslav side? Do you remember perhaps?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was Mr. Todorovic, also Mr. Korac after him and now it's Mr. Gagic, three persons have been at that post since that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts with Berislav Pusic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did. He was the president of the commission of Herceg Bosna. As you know, there were three commissions active in the territory of Bosnia and Hercegovina, the Herceg Bosna commission, the Federation commission, or rather Bosna, that was their name at the time, and the commission of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you know that he is in one of the courtrooms here and that he is being held responsible for, amongst other things, for his work in the commission?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't really following what he was saying in the courtroom. I don't know whether that relates to his work on these topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, did your commission from the time that you were at its head, and perhaps you know about the period from before, ever participate in the exchange of civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we did. And you can see that from the number of persons released from prisons and camps, as well as their affiliation, whether they were members of the armed forces or whether they were civilians. Our assignment, our main task, was on the basis of available information, and this was the work of other commissions as well, to make lists in order to free those persons from prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was an exchange ever executed through the commissions that were -- of civilians who were not in camps of one side or the other?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not involving Republika Srpska, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You talked about persons that were captured in Croatia and taken to camps in Serbia, you provided charts and tables with information on that. What I'm interested in is the following: In negotiations when you're negotiating with the other side, you receive information that you seek for example such and such a person is being sought from Bosnia or Serbia, that, for example, went missing or disappeared in Bosnia. When you establish information and you, for example, establish that the person is in the lower prison in Split or in Osijek or in Brod, depending on where the prison was, did you ever check how was it possible that a person from Bosnia found themselves in prison in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that was in our jurisdiction, to make that kind of check, and you can see on the basis of regulations that our main assignment was the release of prisoners, the release and exchange of prisoners. You can speculate how come this happened, but a number of situations were possible. It happened that people happened to be captured on the line of separation or that they were caught when they were visiting another territory. This is something that happened often, that people were captured in the inter-boundary areas between states too, between Hungary and Yugoslavia. These situations are possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you something specific, and you were asked this in the Milosevic case and perhaps relates to a period when you were not in the position. Do you have information about the existence of the camp Odzak? When after the Croats left the territory of Odzak, all the prisoners, there were hundreds of them, perhaps even a thousand of them, and they were all transferred to camps or prisons in Croatia? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know specifically the situation for Odzak. I don't know where those people were transferred, but I know that there were situations when - and this is what I mentioned before - people were in the boundary area, members of the armed forces were withdrawing, they crossed into the territory of Croatia, and that is when they brought prisoner of war with them who, as such, were recorded and registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 22, line 18, I mentioned --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if you allow me, I been doing this work from 1993, so I am competent to discuss this topic from that time on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am going back to this period, because you spoke -- you are speaking about Vukovar, which is 1991.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm talking about the records that I am maintaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is that your commission, or actually not just the commission, but your function was to monitor the situation in the camps in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To monitor the situation in terms of conditions, of accommodation, and the health of the detainees. This is what our task was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you though that if you have information about Croatian citizens that were in Serb camps, I'm sure that you received information from the other commissions when they were seeking persons, that you received information that persons from Bosnia were in your camps and did you -- when you found out such information, did you inform your authorised organs, ministries, and so on, that in your camps there were persons who were foreign nationals. This is the question, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not in our mandate to inform that. Our -- them about that. Our mandate was to secure the release of persons, and this was very clear. I, or no one in that position could not exceed their mandate, which was regulated by the pertinent regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Although you didn't take part in it, you were informed about the large exchange in Nemetin on the 14th of August, 1991. We're interested in that because there were many people from Vukovar who even testified here who were involved in that exchange. Are you aware that on that occasion in Nemetin, your commission, the Croatian Exchange Commission for Detainees and Missing Persons, exchanged 62 persons who were captured on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are you aware of that information?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they were detained, but I know that they were exchanged, that these people were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The date of that exchange is the 14th of August, 1992. I correct myself.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to say one thing in relation to that exchange. The exchange was agreed on in Budapest with representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross, and the exchange was not conducted by using the first and last names of person or their ethnic affiliation or their citizenship, it was conducted on the basis of the basic humanitarian principle, all for all. Therefore, it is very clear that all the people, regardless of where they were captured, were transferred or were included in the process of that particular exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the name Dragutin Lesic mean anything to you, whose cremated remains were handed over to you by the exchange commission. He was cremated at Ernestinovo, at Ernestinovo.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't remember that. I think this is something quite different. What it was, if that's the same case, but I'm not sure if it's the last surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dragutin Lesic from Novi Grad, near Odzak?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a fact that these remains were handed over, and these remains were cremated together with other remains not at the camp. Since there was no information, the mortal remains were kept at the institute for forensic medicine, no information was available. There were some other mortal remains, social cases, welfare cases, and on the basis of the findings of the commission, affiliated with the Ministry of Health. Such mortal remains that are held for more than a year and their origin is not known and there is nobody to receive these mortal remains, these mortal remains are cremated and all of this is recorded. When we found out at the negotiations that such a possibility existed, we carried out some checks, we established that this is what occurred and in accordance with -- on the basis of agreement via the commission with the family, we handed over the mortal remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we're going move to the main topic of this examination. I'm going to deal with two categories, the category of detainees and missing persons -- actually of expelled and missing persons and then I also wanted to clarify some facts with you. Your database, as the basis of all the analysis is based on the census conducted in 1991. This was in March 1991, when the results were published and I think that the census was actually conducted in 1990, perhaps I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is based on the population census; it's the only relevant population census that exists from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was the census that was done for the whole territory of the then Yugoslavia that was the last census, there was another census that was carried out in Croatia in 2001 but that was a new census using new territorial units?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the territorial approach was different and I don't have that information with me right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What my learned friend Mr. Vasic asked you, and I'm going to ask you that question, and it's based on some theoretical grounds, the statistical information given by territorial units at the time of the census of 1991, was something that you compared with the situation in 2001, and using the territorial divisions at that time. So having conducted the analysis the way you did, why didn't you conduct the same analysis using the territorial division from 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps then and now we misunderstood each other. When I spoke about the information, information for the Podunavlje region, I said that the information was compiled for the region that was occupied at the time, according to each particular settlement, and this information relates to the occupied part of the territory. This is what we're talking about, the districts that were not under the control of the Republic of Croatia or rather its institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but I would like to clarify the following: For example, let us take the town of Vukovar. You have information from 1991, statistical data, which, for you, is the basis for all your analysis. When you were doing your analysis at the time, did you take the boundaries of Vukovar that were administratively enforced in 1991 or later?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for one thing. That is the number of displaced persons in Vukovar. Because the office for displaced persons included information for additional four settlements, but there was explained in this section. So the analysis of the population was made on that basis, so that we do have the correct information. The basis is the year 1991, the lists were made settlement by settlement, and the results were reached so that all those settlements which were not under the control of the Republic of Croatia were included in the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I found information that about eight per cent of the population at the time was on temporary employment abroad from the Vukovar area, so those people who were registered as residing in Vukovar were actually at that time, and for who knows how long, abroad. What was the approach to that particular category of citizens regardless of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were included in the census, then they were proper residents and nobody could say whether they were living abroad or not. This is the category of people temporarily employed abroad, temporarily, so their domicile, their legal domicile was in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although factually speaking they could have been abroad for many years?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen, somebody can go for medical treatment and stay there for several years and not be recorded in the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at document 280 on the 65 ter list, ERN number 3448008 [as interpreted], page 30 and 31. This is the census, and this is one of the agreed facts in this case. I'm now interested in one category of data. You may have it. Do you know how many persons in this census of 1991 were undeclared?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean for entire Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Croatia, or Podunavlje and Vukovar, the town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people should fall under the category "others." And that category was added to all tables, both in percentages and figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. So category "others." And your number for Vukovar residents who were displaced were 14.31 per cent?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we get to that I will clarify all data for you. But in all instances where we have the category "others," that category covers all those who did not declare their ethnic background. But this category also includes some ethnic minorities that did not exist as separate categories anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have a document, it's going to come up on the screen. One matter I find quite interesting, and if you know, please answer. Do you know that in the territory of entire Yugoslavia in 1981 there was a large number of Yugoslavs, and then in the 1991 census their number decreased sharply. Are you familiar with this piece of information, namely that many people who declare themselves as Yugoslavs in 1981 later on changed their national orientation and declared themselves in different terms at the later census?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen, everybody has the freedom of choice; it was guaranteed in the constitution. It is clear that, yes, there was such a phenomenon, and we can look into its origin, but if we're now dealing with facts and the fact is that that's what the situation was in 1991, then you will see that the figures shown in these tables reflect the situation in the entire Yugoslavia, and this was done by the then Federal Bureau for Statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that in 1990 and 1991, in the territory of the entire Yugoslavia it was quite unpopular to declare oneself as a Yugoslav and that it was a notorious fact?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, why would that have been unpopular. People probably had other motives, and I don't see why that is important. Do you know how census was conducted? It was done in such a way that the questionnaires were filled privately so everybody has an opportunity to declare themselves freely, and they did so. And people can of course comment this in any way they wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't going to go into detailed analysis of this document, and I see that it's not on the screen yet. I want it to be tendered into evidence. Even though the national composition is not a disputed fact, I still wanted to have this tendered into evidence. I hope the OTP won't object to have this document, 285 -- or rather, I correct myself, 280 from the 65 ter list, be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document has many pages. This is the census data. What's important for me is that there are various categories and differences in these categories over the years. How many people declared themselves as certain ethnic group. I would like to have this in the evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 561, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we're going turn to displaced persons, which is a category that you analysed. We will see now something in Power Point, a document that we received from the OTP. Mr. Grujic, we received this diskette from the OTP. You have the document on your screen. We don't have a similar table relating to the displaced persons in the evidence. That's why I'm -- would like to know whether it was your service or your rather your state that delivered this document to the Prosecution, the one that you can see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was my understanding. Because this document exists both in the B/C/S and in English. Your service translated these documents into English; isn't that right? So they provided both the B/C/S and the English version?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I see that you used the term "displaced persons" in this document for the word "prognani" in B/C/S. I don't know whether you speak English, but I would like to know whether this is the version produced by your state.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This issue was debated in other cases as well. This is the issue of translation. I can confirm that several words I used for this term prognani, we used the term prognani and izbegli. These are two basic terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will get to that, and I think it will be best to look into regulation rather than into grammar to define these two terms. But at any rate, this is the document that your country produced in English, and submitted it to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was produced by me personally, or rather submitted by me personally. And if you wish we can clarify whatever you think needs to be clarified. If there is a problem in translation, I think we can deal with it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, we won't go into grammar, we will rather look at the concepts and notions. What the OTP disclosed to us, and what was tendered into evidence in documents 5542 and 5543, there is the translation into English in these documents disclosed by the Prosecution and the term "expelled persons" is used there. And I think we need to clarify this. Both this document and the document we received as the official translation, the term "displaced persons" is used, and I would like to clarify this with the witness so that we can sure whether this is a grammatical issue or an essential, meaning issue. When you testified on the 1st of June on page 9.933, you spoke of the persons who were forced to leave their residence and you said to those were prognani or displaced persons. We're now dealing with the data at the level of Croatia which says that there were 220.338 persons who are categorised as prognani or displaced persons, and are you claiming that this many people were forced to leave their residence, that the force was used? Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we need to clarify this. What does it mean, forced? What does it mean that the force was used? That means that either the force was used or there was a threat. It also means that these people were in such a mental state that they had to leave their homes and that they were unable to return to their homes because nobody could guarantee their safety. This is how we see this term.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will get to the definition, but this is how you see it, this is how you define the term "prognani"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, let's clarify something. The office for displaced persons, which is the official institution dealing with this issue, defines displaced person as people who had to leave their homes for the reasons I explained and who are in the free territory of the Republic of Croatia. So these are prognani, displaced persons. Refugees are people who came from other countries to the Republic of Croatia or people from the Republic of Croatia to the territory of other countries, so there is a significant difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we fully agree there, that the term prognani, or displaced person, is somebody who moved from one place to another, but only within one state and that refugees are people who crossed the state border. But I want to ask you about your definition of displaced persons because you seem to define it as people who left because of force, use of force or threat of force. You said that for that reason people left their residence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for those reasons or for their subjective perception of un -- lack of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's another issue.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but these are facts. I know where this debate will lead. We can get directly to the point, we don't need to beat around the bush. Let us put things in proper context. You are now referring to operations for -- Flash and Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. No, not at all. Those questions were put to you in other trials. I have no questions pertaining to 1995.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to read the degree on the status of displaced persons and refugees. I think there won't be any need to tender this into evidence. We will just put one copy in front of the witness. I have already informed the OTP about that, and I think that we will see how competent technical services define these categories, displaced persons and refugees. [In English] Mr. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Grujic, I will read this out slowly. This is a decree on the status of displaced person and refugees of the government of Croatia, dated the 27th of October, 1991. I suppose that your office functions pursuant to this decree. I apologise, the date was 1992. Article 2: "A person who independently or in an organised way via a municipal Crisis Staff, municipal civil protection staff, Croatian Red Cross, or a centre for social work, had to leave the territory -- its residence in the territory of the state of Croatia in order to escape from an immediate life-threatening condition to escape an armed aggression or an armed operation, such a person can be awarded the status of a displaced person or a refugee." The next sentence: "A displaced person in this decree is a person described in paragraph 1 of this article, a person who fled from one area of the Republic of Croatia to another area of the Republic of Croatia, whereas a refugee is a person from the paragraph 1 of this article who went abroad." Following this, a law was adopted. Did I read this out correctly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A law was adopted on the status of displaced persons and refugees, we're going to look at Article 2, it was adopted on the 6th of October, 1993, so about a year after this decree. The law defines these persons in Article 2: "A person who moved from an area of the territory of Croatia that was in a war zone who moved either independently or in an organised fashion through the municipal Crisis Staff, Croatian Red Cross, social work centre or any other organisations. And a person who based on the assessment of the organs of the Ministry of the Interior or a competent command of the Croatian army left their residence in order to escape from life-threatening conditions, to escape from an aggression or other armed operation, shall be given a status of a displaced person or a refugee." And then they go on further to define this identically as in the decree. You will agree with me that when it comes to displaced persons and when your office compiled these statistical data, you used the categories as defined in law, the categories of displaced persons and refugees?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's beyond dispute. But both the law and the decree speak of status, which is a material status and this is how it should be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will be interpreting it here, I'm not asking you to interpret this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know whether we need to tender this into evidence. I don't have English translations provided, but I think that you have the interpreted investigation and perhaps you can take judicial notice of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think we need judicial notice, we have sufficient of it in the transcript. In English for most purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am quite satisfied with the English interpretation. I think it's time for a break and then perhaps we can continue afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now, resuming in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just read one more thing from the regulations. Do you have this regulation in front of you that I gave you, Mr. Grujic? This is Article 13. The regulation that we talked about yesterday about -- earlier about the status of refugees and displaced person, Article 13 says: "A person awarded or granted the status of displaced person will be provided with accommodation; two, food; three, assistance in social adjustment; four, schooling for their children; five, health coverage; and six, assistance to cover all other essential living expenses or requirements." I would just like to add under three, it was assistance in social adjustment and psychological help, that was not recorded. Mr. Grujic, I'm going to ask you about what it says in the regulation. I assume that these are all the benefits once a person is granted the status of a displaced person, it's something that is provided by the state; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we're going to move to the tables and charts. I would like to look at Exhibit 545, Mr. Grujic. That is tab -- I would like to find it. It's tab 2.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the transcript, I would just like it to be noted that as far as the translations are concerned that we received from the Prosecution and which have been tendered as evidence, are used and that is the word "expelled" should be used for the term prognani.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. I believe that the word that was used in the original reports should be used. And that should be the term "displaced." Exhibits 541, 542 and 545, but this is something that we will also take up with the CLSS. The exhibits which have been tendered are draft translations done by the Prosecution, and all the previous translations which are official Tribunal translations use the term "displaced." I assume that we're going to get this from CLSS later?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, now we're going to look at this table, the table that relates to Vukovar. First of all, we have the national composition of inhabitants, is that correct, from 1991. You explained what you said earlier to me, that the percentage 14.31 per cent or 6.390 persons are all those persons who were not included in the categories where people declared themselves according to their ethnic groups, so these would all be the national or ethnic minorities?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ethnic minorities that are not mentioned in the previous categories.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This number, 44.639, of displaced -- actually, no. Of citizens of the town, these are 44.639 inhabitants, and the town is viewed in its original administrative boundaries?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when we say Vukovar, we also include Borovo Naselje; that would be the territorial boundary at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This number, 22.165, refers to the displaced person which you received for the displaced persons, returnees, and refugees?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the officially registered number of persons from the territory of the town of Vukovar, and Lipovaca, Sotin, and Grabovo are added to that figure. These how they maintained their records.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that how it is written down here, and this is the data that was received from that administration. My question is, did you seek, did you receive, did you have at any point in time, persons whose place of residence was Vukovar, they left Vukovar but did not report to that administration, they perhaps reported to some other state?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we are explicitly talking about the category of people here who, as you yourself said, have been granted the status of displaced persons and who reported to the institution which is maintaining these figures and behind each of those numbers there is a card certifying their displaced status.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is how I understood it. But you don't know how many persons there are there who had left Vukovar but did not report to anyone in that period?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. If they reported to somewhere else, how can we know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have information, how many citizens in Vukovar lived there while it was not, let me put it this way, under your sovereignty in that period from 1991 until 1998?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's clear that we cannot have such data.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps somebody kept this -- these figures. Could you have asked, perhaps, the Vukovar municipal administration for information like that, or the East Krajina Autonomous Area, do you know how many people lived in Vukovar when it was not in your sovereignty?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the numbers are different there, and that is precisely the reason why we did not go into that, we have people leaving, people coming back, there are a lot of people coming in and out of that area passing through, so it would be very difficult to have such information. On the other hand this is data that will be classified in the future, in the way that it should be done. At this point in time, I can speak about official records and official information that is in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Official information from your administration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is official data of the Republic of Croatia, from institutions which, in the Republic of Croatia, deal with this subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I'm going to ask you something else. Table number 2, and this is the number of the expelled, according to the time of expulsion, up until the 18th of November, 1991, you established that 14.043 persons were expelled from Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this is the period from the census until the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from the census. We said at the beginning, when the first expelled person or displaced person in the Republic of Croatia was registered, and then we can start from that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I correct myself. You didn't say that right at the beginning, but only on the second day of your testimony. That was when you mentioned your -- that category, you said that the first person that was displaced was in March, 1991. Perhaps we can refer to that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first displaced person was registered on the 2nd of January, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is the following: You place the cut-off date on the 18th of November, 1991, for this particular figure. Can you tell me how many people of this number were granted the status of displaced persons until August 1st, 1991, and how many of them were granted this status after August 1st, 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you such a figure. The statistics that you see here are statistics that were drawn up by the office for completely different needs, and they are what they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to tell you why I'm asking you about these dates. We know that here in this courtroom, because these are the dates that we are dealing with in the document that we call the indictment, but this is what this is all about. Here, before this Trial Chamber, we have heard that the town of Vukovar was under blockade from late September, 1991, and this would be testimony on page 1.354 of 9th of May, for the reference of the Trial Chamber. So you are not able to rule out the possibility that these 40-odd thousand people left Vukovar before the blockade, because witnesses have said that after that nobody was able to leave. So you cannot rule this possible out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can rule it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you give me your arguments?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over 4.000 people, I cannot give you the exact number, but I do assert that over 4.000 people from Vukovar through Mitrovica, we're not talking about prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But this is after the 18th, this is a different category, and we will discuss this later. This is the category after the 18th of November. This is the next group. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question was whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was, these 14.000 people who left Vukovar before the 18th of November, 1991, in relation to them, can you rule out the possibility that they all left before the 1st of September, 1991, because we have information, actually before the end of September. We have information that in late September, 1991, the town was blockaded, and nobody was able to leave anymore. This is the testimony. So based on this testimony I am asking you: If the town was blockaded, is it possible that these people left the town before the blockade?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them for sure. There was the possibility to leave town, as far as I know. It wasn't very easy, but it did exist. So I really cannot speak about this. I would like to speak about facts and the numbers that I have presented here. The dates are what they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that in relation to the number of 14.043 persons who left Vukovar before the 18th of November, 1991, according to reports from your office, you are unable to say when they left exactly, if we look at it in the frame of reference of January, 1991 onwards?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is very easy to see. You have all the records. But I could not analyse each card and each person one by one, we're talking about statistical figures, not personal data for individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right, very well. We have heard many testimonies here from people who, regardless of their ethnic background, sent their families away before the combat began in Vukovar, so my question is, if a person left their home before the start of combat operations, because they were afraid people began to disappear and so on, and that person left for Zagreb and then four months later after November 1991 said, "I left Vukovar in April 1991 but my house now is destroyed. I don't have anywhere to go back to," would that person be granted the status of a displaced person if the person from January received it, I assume that such a person would get it too.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You saw that there was a decree specifying the circumstances under which one could become a displaced person, gain that status. So whoever fulfilled the requirements was granted that status and those who did not meet the requirements did not receive that status.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood it. Now I will turn to this other category that you touched upon, which were displaced persons from the 18th of November, 1991, until the 1st of May, 1992. You gave us the figure of 5.346 persons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These are the convoys that went to Sremska Mitrovica, then they came back, there were some problems, people were taken to Nustar, this was a large convoy on or around the 20th of November. We heard a lot of testimony about that. I suppose that the majority of these persons left in that period of time, you said it was over 4.000 persons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about 4.000 persons went through this transit area. These were not prisoners of war. People went through Sremska Mitrovica and then via Bosnia they were repatriated back to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in those days the JNA offered all citizens to go where they wished to go, whoever wished to go to Serbia could go there and whoever wished to go to Croatia could go there as well, regardless of their ethnic background. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't testify to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But do you know that the JNA made this offer that whoever wanted to remain in Vukovar could stay there? This is what we heard from witnesses.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I can't testify to that because I don't know. I can only give you second-hand information about what I heard from somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why I'm asking you this, I'm asking because we saw that in the reports when somebody reported a missing person certain information was provided. So I guess when somebody filled paperwork to be given the status of a displaced person, then that person also needed to provide some information, so I'm just interested in knowing whether anybody mentioned that the JNA had offered people to stay in Vukovar if they so wished. Do you know anything about that and such data?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. And I can't testify about that. I don't rule that out as a possibility, but I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We know that European observer mission and International Red Cross also was involved and filled some paperwork, and I assume that your service, which existed under a different name at the time, also received some information from international organisations?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the extent that it was feasible, in view of the date. Because, as you know, all international organisations within their mandate, have certain limitations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, not in view of the date, but in view of the mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have 14.000 people in one category and five odd thousand in another category, and out of those figures, you don't know people, when filling paperwork of their status, said that they left because they were expelled by the JNA. You don't know anything about the circumstances of them leaving?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were those questionnaires that I provided, and they specify similar data, everything that people filled in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this questionnaire resembles the one for missing persons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All the information that was relevant in order to obtain a certain status was entered into specific questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you don't know approximately how many claimed that they had been expelled by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, I need to reorganise my notes. We will now turn to Exhibit 542, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you move on, Mr. Lukic, a couple of things that the Chamber would like clarified. I wonder, the information in your records when you have identified somebody as being displaced or a refugee, is that information based on a questionnaire filled in by the person, or is it on information obtained from various agencies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, solely on the basis of a report, any person that reported themselves as a refugee or a displaced person had to fill a questionnaire. Only after the questionnaire was filled could that person obtain a status of a refugee or a displaced person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the date upon which that person left Vukovar, in this case, is that the date which they say was the time they actually left Vukovar, or was that the date that their category was recognised, when they had completed the questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was done in such a way that every displaced person, upon filling a questionnaire, was entitled to certain rights. Those people who were expelled had to live somewhere, had to obtain food somewhere, and the state agencies gave them housing and so on. So they had to fill a questionnaire and the time period between them leaving their houses and filling questionnaire was a very brief one. Each such person filled in the date when they left home. They had to find shelter and the state provided them accommodation and they filled the questionnaires there and were then sent to other provisional accommodation, either individual or collective, once, and received certain benefits from the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That was the date on which they were recorded the date they said they had left Vukovar, or is it the date when they were registered as displaced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the moment they were registered, because the questionnaire specifies the date of registration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we'll turn to Exhibit 542, which is tab 2.6 for Vukovar-Srijem county. Once again we will focus on this category of displaced persons. Have you found that, Mr. Grujic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you reported that in Vukovar-Srijem county from the total number of residents, based on the 1991 census, which was 111.248 residents, there were a total of 55.644 displaced or expelled persons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then you created two categories for this time period while they were displaced. One was, say, from January, 1991, until the 1st of May, 1992. And in this county the number of such persons was 47.137 persons, we're interested in this period of time because of our indictment. Is this right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, out of this number, which goes all the way up until May 1992, can you tell me how many people in this county were registered as leaving the county before the 1st of August, 1991, or the 1st of September, 1991? I'm interested in those periods. Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat that all statistics were done based on the same criteria.
